messages.subject: Re: Using generic lists in Renjin
parts:
Hi Anton,
R can be tricky to wrap your head around when first coming from a different language. It helps a lot to think of R as "a lisp" - there's a bit of extra syntax thrown into make it look a bit more like fortran, but in the end it's all parens!

Have you seen the page on "moving data between R and Java" ?
http://docs.renjin.org/en/latest/moving-data-between-java-and-r-code.html#pulling-data-from-r-into-java

You might also look at the general documentation for the javax.script API:
http://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/scripting/programmer_guide/

If your "Person" bean has the normal getters and setters, then you should be able to pass the List<Person> into Renjin and then, you can certainly use familiar java idioms such as:

sum <- 0
for(p in persons) {
    sum <- sum + p$age
}
avg <- sum / length(persons)

But then of course you will miss out on the power of R as an array language. You can turn your list into an "atomic vector" by using idioms from R's functional side:

age <- sapply(persons, function(p) { return p$age })

If you do print(age), then you'll see something like this:

> print(age)
[1] 14 3 25 52  1  

You could do the same for other properties of your bean

> name <- sapply(persons, function(p) p$name)
> print(name)
[1] "Bob"  "Karl" "Sam"

Then you can use R's more fluent functions:

> mean(age)


And so on...

HTH

Alex

parts:
Hi Anton,

Maybe you could take a look at SciCom.  SciCom is a Ruby wrapper for Renjing, but since SciCom targets JRuby (JVM), at the end it is all Java, and thus can be packed in a jar and served through a web server.  

When I started SciCom, my first idea was to actually interface with Renjin SEXP, but then I realized that much of R power could be lost if I tried that, as R is very dynamic and can deal with heterogeneous inputs. For instance, arrays of different dimensions that get dynamically expanded according to some R rules.  At the end, SciCom "just" translates Ruby syntax to R strings (that the user never sees) and calls eval.  For the user, it seems that she is coding in Ruby, on the background, it is all just R code.

If you have questions, feel free to contact me.


Cheers,


Rodrigo
